[0:04] If you've ever tried to make an AI model, talk to your tools or your data, you've probably realized something. It's messy. Every API behaves differently, every integration needs custom code, and every time the model changes, your connection breaks. The model context protocol, or MCP, was created to fix exactly that. By the end of this video, you'll understand what the model context protocol actually is, why it exists, and how it's changing the way models interact with the world.
[0:36] We'll walk through the core ideas step by step, see how it compares to traditional APIs, and talk about what this means for developers, building agents, or AI powered applications. So what is the model context protocol. At its core, MCP is an open standard for connecting models to tools, data, and context in a really consistent and structured way. You can think of it as a shared language between models and the systems around them. It defines how a model can discover available tools,
[1:09] ask for information, and perform actions without having to know the specific implementation details behind each one. This protocol was introduced by Anthropic and is now being adopted across the industry because it solves one of the biggest pain points in AI development today. How to make models use external resources safely and reliably. So here's why that matters. APIs were never designed for AI models. They were designed for programs that already know exactly what they want, programs
[1:41] that can form precise, deterministic requests. A language model doesn't work that way. It generates text probabilistically. It reasons about uncertain inputs and often needs to ask questions, clarify or explore before it knows what to do. MCP bridges that gap. It gives models a structured way to discover and describe the resources they can use. So things like functions, data sets, documents or prompts are all available through a consistent interface.
[2:14] Instead of hard coding every integration, the model can now dynamically query what's available, use it, and even chain multiple tools together, so all while staying within a safe, standardized framework to understand how MCP actually works, let's unpack the main idea. The protocol defines two sides clients and servers. The client is usually the language model or the agent system that wants to perform a task, something like Cloud, Gemini app or an agent built on top of OpenAI
[2:48] or Google's frameworks. The server is the environment that exposes resources that the model can use a database, a file system, a company's internal tools or even a document search engine. When the client connects to the server, the server doesn't just respond with data. Instead, it advertises what capabilities it supports, what resources exist, what actions can be taken, and what inputs are required. This means the model doesn't need
[3:19] to be pre-programmed with every API or every endpoint. It can dynamically discover them. The communication between these two sides happens through a really simple and well-defined schema. The client sends requests like list available resources, call this action, or retrieve this data. The server then responds with a structured JSON describing what's possible and what happened. That's the essence of MCP, a standardized way for models to talk to their environment.
[3:50] Now let's go a bit deeper. Technically, the MCP protocol defines a few main resource types tools, prompts, resources, and context that together form what the model can see and use. Tools are actions that the model can invoke. For example, a tool could be a search database, send email, or even analyze a file. Resources are pieces of data and state like a text document or database role, or even an image. Prompts are reusable templates that
[4:21] describe how the model should behave for specific tasks, and context represents external information that the model can pull into its reasoning process. Things like recent chat history, company data, or user preferences. When an MCP client connects, it can request a list of all of these things from the server. Each tool or resource comes with metadata that describes what it does, what input it expects, and what output it returns. This allows models to interact intelligently.
[4:53] The protocol enforces a consistent schema across all tools. So whether the model is using a GitHub server, a CRM server or a calendar server, it speaks the same language. Now let's address the big question. If we already have APIs, why do we need MCP at all. The answer comes down to who the consumer is. APIs were designed for programs written by humans. MCP is designed for models that reason like humans.
[5:24] You can think of MCP as an abstraction above APIs. APIs still exist. MCP just makes them model friendly. Under the hood, your MCP server might still call your existing REST or GraphQL APIs, but the model never sees that it only interacts through the structured MCP schema, which handles discovery, validation, and execution in a uniform way. That's what makes MCP powerful. It lets you expose your system to any compliant model
[5:57] without custom integrations each time. Let's take a practical example. Say you're building a personal assistant agent that can check your calendar, pull meeting notes, and draft follow up emails. In the old world, you would integrate with Google Calendar, notion, and Gmail APIs. You'd write code for each service, handle authentication, rate limits, and all of the weird edge cases. Then you teach the model how to use those endpoints through really long, fragile system prompts with MCP.
[6:29] You build or install servers for each of those systems a calendar server, a node server, an email server. Each one advertises what it can do. The model automatically sees the available tools like list events, get meeting summary, or send email. It can reason about what to use, in what order and what data to pass between them. The key difference is that the developer doesn't have to write glue code for each new tool. The model knows how to interact because the protocol is
[7:00] consistent. That's the kind of simplicity that MCP brings to AI development. So this shift is already underway, the same way that HTTP unified the web. MCP is already beginning to unify how models talk to tools. And that's why learning it now matters. Because soon every serious AI developer will need to know how to make their systems MCP aware. [0:00] Intro: The speaker introduces Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, explaining that they are simple programs providing AI models like Claude, Cursor, and ChatGPT a list of standard functions they are allowed to execute.
[0:30] Concept Overview: The speaker explains that LLMs cannot natively access local files or databases, relying on structured tool declarations with names, parameters, and descriptions to send text-based tool execution requests back to code.
[1:00] Function Calling Mechanism: The speaker illustrates how an LLM requests a tool call via text, which application code executes before returning the formatted output back to the model for context processing.
[1:30] Problem Before MCP: The speaker highlights how custom tool plumbing previously had to be rewritten for every specific LLM and application, creating fragmentation across different AI tools and integrations.
[2:00] MCP Definition: The speaker introduces Model Context Protocol as a unified standard, describing it as a "USB-C for AI tools" that allows tools to be written once and used anywhere.
[2:30] MCP Architecture: The speaker outlines the two-sided architecture of MCP, distinguishing between the server hosting tool definitions and client applications like Claude Desktop or Cursor executing model interactions.
[3:00] Local Execution Mode: The speaker explains local MCP server execution, where the client application directly launches the server as a local sub-process using standard input/output (stdio) piping.
[3:30] Remote Execution Mode: The speaker describes remote MCP server execution over HTTP, which allows servers hosted on external URLs to be accessed by multiple users across different devices.
[4:00] Production Considerations: The speaker discusses trade-offs, pointing out that while remote HTTP deployment is preferred for production apps, it introduces network access control challenges absent in local stdio setups.
[4:30] Access Control Questions: The speaker outlines the three critical access control questions required for remote server requests: caller identity, user permission authorization, and on-whose-behalf actions are performed.
[5:00] Security Audit Risks: The speaker shares security audit findings showing that many public MCP servers lack authentication or rely on fragile static API keys shared across multiple agents.
[5:30] Recommended Auth Specification: The speaker explains why the official MCP specification recommends standard OAuth 2.1 with PKCE instead of static API keys for secure, user-bound agent access control.
[6:00] OAuth 2.1 Flow: The speaker details how unauthenticated client requests trigger a 401 Unauthorized response containing an authorization server URL, initiating a browser-based user login screen.
[6:30] User Consent and Tokens: The speaker shows how users authenticate, approve permission scopes on a consent screen, and issue access tokens that clients attach to subsequent tool invocation requests.
[7:00] Token Validation: The speaker explains how remote MCP servers validate token signatures, audience claims, and permission scopes before executing requested functions on behalf of authenticated users.
[7:30] Dynamic Client Registration: The speaker introduces Dynamic Client Registration, explaining how AI clients dynamically register with authorization servers to streamline user sign-in flows automatically.
[8:00] Token Scopes: The speaker describes permission scopes like `notes:read` and `notes:write`, explaining how granular scopes enforce fine-grained access control over specific server tools and actions.
[8:30] Transition to Code: The speaker transitions to the code demonstration, outlining plans to build a local stdio server, convert it to remote HTTP, and add full OAuth security.
[9:00] Spec Documentation: On-screen, the speaker reviews the official Model Context Protocol specification website, detailing JSON-RPC messaging standards and basic protocol architecture concepts.
[9:30] Protocol Message Patterns: The speaker navigates through sequence diagrams in the spec, showing standardized request-response patterns, capability negotiation, and error handling structures.
[10:00] Python Setup: In VS Code, the speaker introduces `FastMCP` framework setup alongside a local SQLite helper script (`notes_db.py`) for managing database notes.
[10:30] Database Helper Functions: The speaker reviews Python functions written to connect to SQLite and perform basic CRUD operations like listing, adding, and deleting stored note records.
[11:00] Defining MCP Tools: The speaker demonstrates wrapping Python functions with `@mcp.tool()` decorators, using docstrings to populate tool descriptions and type hints to specify parameter types.
[11:30] Local Server Entrypoint: The speaker shows `mcp.run()`, explaining that by default `FastMCP` runs locally over standard input/output (stdio) as a sub-process spawned by an AI client.
[12:00] Docstrings and Annotations: The speaker emphasizes how type hints and docstrings enrich the JSON schema generated for AI models, improving tool call accuracy during agent reasoning.
[12:30] Tool Schema Registration: The speaker explains how `FastMCP` inspects decorated Python functions to automatically build the MCP-compliant tool manifest sent to connecting client applications.
[13:00] Cursor Settings: The speaker opens Cursor IDE preferences, navigating to the Tools & MCPs section to demonstrate adding a custom local MCP server configuration.
[13:30] Configuring stdio in Cursor: The speaker edits `mcp.json` in Cursor, adding command arguments (`uv run`) and directory paths to launch the local Python script as a sub-process.
[14:00] Connecting Local Server: The speaker saves `mcp.json` and verifies in Cursor settings that the `notes-local` MCP server connects successfully and lists three available tools.
[14:30] Testing Local Tool Calls: In Cursor's AI agent chat window, the speaker prompts the assistant to interact with the notes server, triggering automated local sub-process execution.
[15:00] Reviewing Agent Actions: The speaker inspects the agent chat log, demonstrating how the model invoked `add_a_note` and returned structured confirmation text directly in the chat interface.
[15:30] Querying Local Notes: The speaker asks the AI agent to list all active notes, confirming that `list_my_notes` reads data from the local SQLite database correctly.
[16:00] stdio Limitations: The speaker highlights stdio drawbacks, noting that local sub-processes lack authentication, user isolation, and remote accessibility for external clients or production deployments.
[16:30] Converting to Remote HTTP: The speaker modifies `mcp.run()` parameters in `v2_remote.py` to use `transport="http"` on port 8000, switching from stdio to an HTTP server.
[17:00] Starting HTTP Server: The speaker runs `v2_remote.py` in the terminal using `uv run`, launching a Uvicorn ASGI server hosting the MCP endpoint at `localhost:8000/mcp`.
[17:30] Updating Cursor to HTTP: In Cursor's `mcp.json`, the speaker replaces the sub-process command with an HTTP URL configuration pointing to `http://localhost:8000/mcp`.
[18:00] Testing HTTP Requests: The speaker verifies connection logs in the terminal as Cursor sends HTTP requests to the running server and successfully executes note commands via network requests.
[18:30] Remote HTTP Benefits: The speaker explains how HTTP transport enables multi-client access, allowing tools to be accessed simultaneously from laptops, mobile apps, or third-party AI agents.
[19:00] Security Risks of Unauthenticated HTTP: The speaker points out that raw HTTP without auth allows anyone with the URL to read, write, or delete notes without permission or identity checks.
[19:30] Production Security Needs: The speaker reiterates that production MCP servers require authentication, authorization scopes, and user-isolated data access to protect sensitive backend APIs.
[20:00] Advert / Sponsor: Advert for Descope Agentic Identity Hub, a sponsor service offering identity management, OAuth 2.1 authorization, consent screens, and token storage for AI agents and MCP.
[20:30] Descope Platform Features: The speaker highlights Descope capabilities, including visual authentication flows, dynamic client registration, token verification SDKs, and third-party API token vaults.
[21:00] Creating Descope Project: In the Descope web console, the speaker creates a new project named "tutorial" to set up an authorization server for the MCP application.
[21:30] Agentic Identity Hub Console: The speaker navigates to Agentic Identity Hub -> MCP Servers in the Descope dashboard to configure authorization settings for the Python server.
[22:00] Registering MCP Server: The speaker creates a new MCP server entry in Descope, specifying the server name `notes` and public endpoint URL `http://localhost:8000/mcp`.
[22:30] Defining Scopes in Descope: The speaker adds custom permission scopes `notes.read` and `notes.write`, providing end-user descriptions that will display on the OAuth consent screen.
[23:00] Obtaining Well-Known URL: The speaker enables Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) and copies the generated Descope well-known OAuth 2.1 configuration URL.
[23:30] Setting Environment Variables: The speaker saves `DESCOPE_CONFIG_URL` and `MCP_SERVER_URL` into the `.env` file to configure the Python server authentication code.
[24:00] Implementing Descope SDK: In `v3_auth.py`, the speaker imports `DescopeProvider` and `descope_mcp`, connecting FastMCP with Descope's authorization server for automatic token verification.
[24:30] Enforcing Scopes and Claims: The speaker writes a helper function (`get_current_user`) to extract user IDs from verified access tokens and check required scopes before executing actions.
[25:00] User-Isolated Tool Logic: The speaker updates tool functions to pass the authenticated caller's user ID to database queries, ensuring users only access their own notes.
[25:30] Starting Auth Server: The speaker launches `v3_auth.py`, observing in terminal logs that unauthenticated requests from Cursor now receive `401 Unauthorized` responses as expected.
[26:00] Initiating OAuth in Cursor: In Cursor settings, the speaker clicks "Connect" on the `notes` server, triggering Cursor to open the Descope OAuth authorization URL in a browser.
[26:30] Web Authentication Flow: On the Descope login page, the speaker selects "Sign in with Google", completes Google OAuth sign-in, and proceeds to the application consent screen.
[27:00] Granting Permission Scopes: The speaker reviews requested permissions (`notes.read`, `notes.write`), clicks "Authorize", and redirects back to Cursor with an issued access token.
[27:30] Testing Authenticated Tools: Back in Cursor, the speaker tests a prompt that invokes `add_a_note` and `whoami`, verifying successful tool execution with user token claims attached.
[28:00] Inspecting User Claims: The speaker inspects the returned `whoami` payload, confirming the presence of the authenticated user ID, client ID, valid scopes, and token expiration timestamp.
[28:30] Testing User Isolation: The speaker logs out of the MCP server in Cursor settings, then connects again using a different Google account to test multi-tenant data isolation.
[29:00] Verifying Data Isolation: Asking the AI agent to list notes under the second account returns zero notes, proving that database records are strictly isolated by authenticated user ID.
[29:30] Descope Connections Vault: In the Descope console, the speaker highlights the Connections library, showing how to securely store and retrieve user tokens for third-party services like GitHub.
[30:00] Outro: Outro concluding the guide on building secure remote MCP servers in Python, encouraging viewers to review linked repository code, like the video, and subscribe.
</transcript>

Every API behaves differently, every integration needs custom code, and every time the model changes, your connection breaks. The model context protocol, or MCP, was created to fix exactly that. By the end of this video, you'll understand what the model context protocol actually is, why it exists, and how it's changing the way models interact with the world.
[0:36] We'll walk through the core ideas step by step, see how it compares to traditional APIs, and talk about what this means for developers, building agents, or AI powered applications. So what is the model context protocol. At its core, MCP is an open standard for connecting models to tools, data, and context in a really consistent and structured way. You can think of it as a shared language between models and the systems around them. It defines how a model can discover available tools,
[1:09] ask for information, and perform actions without having to know the specific implementation details behind each one. This protocol was introduced by Anthropic and is now being adopted across the industry because it solves one of the biggest pain points in AI development today. How to make models use external resources safely and reliably. So here's why that matters. APIs were never designed for AI models. They were designed for programs that already know exactly what they want, programs
[1:41] that can form precise, deterministic requests. A language model doesn't work that way. It generates text probabilistically. It reasons about uncertain inputs and often needs to ask questions, clarify or explore before it knows what to do. MCP bridges that gap. It gives models a structured way to discover and describe the resources they can use. So things like functions, data sets, documents or prompts are all available through a consistent interface.
[2:14] Instead of hard coding every integration, the model can now dynamically query what's available, use it, and even chain multiple tools together, so all while staying within a safe, standardized framework to understand how MCP actually works, let's unpack the main idea. The protocol defines two sides clients and servers. The client is usually the language model or the agent system that wants to perform a task, something like Cloud, Gemini app or an agent built on top of OpenAI
[2:48] or Google's frameworks. The server is the environment that exposes resources that the model can use a database, a file system, a company's internal tools or even a document search engine. When the client connects to the server, the server doesn't just respond with data. Instead, it advertises what capabilities it supports, what resources exist, what actions can be taken, and what inputs are required. This means the model doesn't need
[3:19] to be pre-programmed with every API or every endpoint. It can dynamically discover them. The communication between these two sides happens through a really simple and well-defined schema. The client sends requests like list available resources, call this action, or retrieve this data. The server then responds with a structured JSON describing what's possible and what happened. That's the essence of MCP, a standardized way for models to talk to their environment.
[3:50] Now let's go a bit deeper. Technically, the MCP protocol defines a few main resource types tools, prompts, resources, and context that together form what the model can see and use. Tools are actions that the model can invoke. For example, a tool could be a search database, send email, or even analyze a file. Resources are pieces of data and state like a text document or database role, or even an image. Prompts are reusable templates that
[4:21] describe how the model should behave for specific tasks, and context represents external information that the model can pull into its reasoning process. Things like recent chat history, company data, or user preferences. When an MCP client connects, it can request a list of all of these things from the server. Each tool or resource comes with metadata that describes what it does, what input it expects, and what output it returns. This allows models to interact intelligently.

[0:04] In this video, we are going to connect an AI agent to an MCP server. You will learn what an MCP server is, why it matters, and how to connect it to your ADK agent. By the end, your agent won't just write and plan, it will also pull from an external tool over MCP. So what exactly is MCP. MCP stands for Model context protocol. That sounds complicated, but here's the simple idea. It's a standard way for agents to talk to external tools.
[0:36] Think of it like a translator. On one side, you have your agent, which is powered by a language model. And on the other side, you might have tools that do very specific things, looking up Google Trends or querying a database or running code. The agent itself can't do these things directly, so MCP sits in the middle. So here's how it works. The tool runs as its own little program, usually in its own process. The agent connects to it over a standard input and output, and then the agent asks, what tools do you have.
[1:08] The MCP server replies with a list of tool names, their arguments, and what they return. Then the agent says, OK, call this tool. With these arguments, the tool runs and the result comes back as JSON. The important part is how cleanly this is separated. Each tool runs in its own process, like its own program. The agent doesn't need to know how the tool is built, what libraries it uses, or even what language it's written in. As long as the tool speaks MCP, the agent can use it.
[1:41] So why is this so powerful. First off, isolation. If a tool crashes, your agent doesn't go down with it. Secondly, it's interoperable. You could write tools in Python go or node and the agent doesn't care. Third, it's discoverable tools describe themselves in schemas so agents can figure out at runtime how to use them. And finally, it's scalable. You can add more tools, swap them out, or version them without rewriting your entire agent code.
[2:11] So if you think of the agent as the brain, MCP is the wire that connects it to its hands and eyes in the real world, the brain decides what to do. MCP carries the request across and the hands do the work. The results come back to the brain. That's the loop that makes agents more than just chatbots. In the last video, we built an agent that writes blog posts. You gave it a topic and it planned out the entire sections, wrote a draft, and even suggested alternative titles.
